ARTICLE: Capital gains tax
WIKIPEDIA REVISION TEXT
======================================================================

{{Short description|Tax on investment profits}}
{{Multiple issues|
{{Update|date=February 2016}}
{{more citations needed|date=December 2019}}
{{Tone|date=February 2020}}
}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=August 2020}}

{{Taxation}}
A '''capital gains tax''' ('''CGT''') is the tax on profits realised on the sale of a non-inventory [[asset]]. The most common [[capital gain]]s are realised from the sale of [[stock]]s, [[Bond (finance)|bonds]], [[precious metal]]s, [[real estate]], and [[property]].

Not all countries impose a capital gains tax, and most have different rates of taxation for individuals compared to corporations.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-05-01 |title=Capital Gains Tax by Country 2026 |url=https://worldpopulationreview.com/country-rankings/capital-gains-tax-by-country |access-date=2026-05-06 |website=World Population Review |language=en}}</ref> Countries that do not impose a capital gains tax include [[Bahrain]], [[Barbados]], the [[Cayman Islands]], the [[Isle of Man]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.iomguide.com/taxation.php|title=Isle of Man Guide – GOVERNMENT, Taxation|website=iomguide.com|access-date=2 February 2019}}</ref> [[Jamaica]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.pwc.com/jm/en/business-in-jamaica/tax-system.jhtml |title=PwC Jamaica |publisher=Pwc.com |access-date=26 September 2018}}</ref> [[New Zealand]], [[Singapore]], and others.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-05-01 |title=Low-tax & tax-free countries for expats 2026: Compare top picks |url=https://www.taxesforexpats.com/articles/immigration/low-tax-countries.html |access-date=2026-05-06 |website=www.taxesforexpats.com}}</ref> In some countries, such as New Zealand and Singapore, professional traders and those who trade frequently are taxed on such profits as a business income.

Capital gains taxes are payable on most valuable items or assets sold at a profit. Antiques, shares, precious metals and second homes could be all subject to the tax if the profit is large enough. This lower boundary of profit is set by the government, and if the profit is lower than this limit it is [[Tax exemption|tax-free]]. The profit is in most cases the difference between the amount (or value) an asset is sold for and the amount it was bought for.

The [[tax rate]] on capital gains may depend on the seller's income. If any property or asset is sold at a loss, it is possible to offset it against annual gains. For [[equities]], national and state legislation often has a large array of fiscal obligations that must be respected regarding capital gains.

==As an obstacle to sale==
The CGT can be considered a cost of selling which can be greater than, for example, [[transaction cost]]s or [[Provision (accounting)|provisions]]. The literature{{what|date=February 2026}} provides information that barriers for trading negatively affects the investors' willingness to trade, which in turn can change asset prices.

Companies with tax-sensitive customers are particularly reactive to capital gains tax and its change. CGT and changes to it affect trading and the stock market. Investors must be ready to react sensibly to these changes, taking into account the cumulative capital gains of their customers. Sales can be delayed due to unfavorable market conditions caused by capital gains tax. A study by Li Jin (2006) showed that a high capital gains tax may discourage selling, though a low capital gains tax can stimulate trade and incentivize investors to sell.<ref name=":1">{{cite journal |last1=Jin |first1=Li |title=Capital Gains Tax Overhang and Price Pressure |journal=The Journal of Finance |date=2006 |volume=61 |issue=3 |pages=1399–1431 |doi=10.1111/j.1540-6261.2006.00876.x |jstor=3699327 }}</ref> "It is easy to show that to be willing to sell now the investor must believe that the stock price will go down permanently. Thus, a capital gains tax can create a potentially large barrier to selling. Of course, the foregoing calculation ignores the possibility that there might be another tax-timing option: Given capital gains tax rates fluctuate over time, it might be worthwhile to time the realization of capital gains and wait until a subsequent regime lowers the capital gains tax rate."<ref name=":1" />

== Locked-in effect ==
Because capital gains are taxed only upon realization, an individual who owns a security that has increased in value may be less likely to sell it. The seller knows that when sold, tax is levied on the positive difference of the price at which the security was bought and the price at sale. If the seller chooses not to sell, the tax is postponed to later date. Postponing allows more time for the security to grow in value and generate returns. If the seller delays the sale, though the absolute value of the tax is greater than if they had not delayed, the [[Present value|present discounted value]] of the tax is reduced; thus allowing the security to grow undoes the tax. Therefore, the seller has an incentive to hold the securities longer than they would have without capital gains tax. This distortion has been called the locked-in effect or lock-in effect.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|last1=Stiglitz|first1=Joseph E.|title=Economics of the Public Sector|last2=Rosengard|first2=Jay K.|publisher=W. W. Norton & Company|year=2015|isbn=9780393937091|pages=653–655}}</ref>

[[Martin Feldstein]], former chairman of the [[Council of Economic Advisers]] under President [[Ronald Reagan|Reagan]] has claimed that the effect is so large that reducing the capital gains tax would lead individuals to sell securities that they previously had refused to sell, to such an extent that government revenues would actually increase.{{citation needed|date=December 2024}} 1994 estimates suggest that a permanent reduction in the capital gains tax rate would have little effect.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Burman |first1=Leonard E. |last2=Randolph |first2=William C. |title=Measuring Permanent Responses to Capital-Gains Tax Changes in Panel Data |journal=The American Economic Review |date=1994 |volume=84 |issue=4 |pages=794–809 |jstor=2118031 }}</ref>

== Investment behaviour ==

=== Asset allocation ===
Capital gains tax systems have been argued to create distortions in portfolio allocation, as investors may favour assets with preferential tax treatment over higher-return investments subject to ordinary income rates.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Stiglitz |first=Joseph E. |date=1983-07-01 |title=Some aspects of the taxation of capital gains |url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0047-2727%2883%2990051-8 |journal=Journal of Public Economics |volume=21 |issue=2 |pages=257–294 |doi=10.1016/0047-2727(83)90051-8 |issn=0047-2727}}</ref> Some analysts observe that this can shift capital toward tax-advantaged vehicles such as municipal bonds or real estate investment trusts even when these offer lower pre-tax returns.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Poterba |first=James M. |date=1987-07-01 |title=How burdensome are capital gains taxes?: Evidence from the United States |url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0047-2727%2887%2990072-7 |journal=Journal of Public Economics |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=157–172 |doi=10.1016/0047-2727(87)90072-7 |issn=0047-2727|hdl=1721.1/63660 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Critics contend that such outcomes reduce economic efficiency by directing capital based on tax considerations rather than underlying economic fundamentals, though proponents of preferential treatment argue it serves legitimate policy goals such as encouraging long-term investment.<ref>{{cite report |url=https://crsreports.congress.gov/product/pdf/R/R41364 |title=Capital Gains Tax Options: Behavioral Responses and Revenues |last=Gravelle |first=Jane G. |date=January 19, 2021 |access-date=2024-01-01 |institution=Congressional Research Service |number=R41364}}</ref>

=== Timing of asset sales ===
Investors may cluster asset sales around tax year boundaries and coordinate disposals with capital losses to minimize tax liability.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Constantinides |first=George M. |date=1983 |title=Capital Market Equilibrium with Personal Tax |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1912150 |journal=Econometrica |volume=51 |issue=3 |pages=611–636 |doi=10.2307/1912150 |jstor=1912150 |issn=0012-9682|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This timing behavior has been associated with periods of reduced transaction volume when tax consequences are unfavorable, and with increased activity when conditions are advantageous.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Vol. 53, No. 5, Oct., 1998 of The Journal of Finance on JSTOR |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/i300838 |access-date=2026-05-19 |website=www.jstor.org |jstor=i300838 |language=en}}</ref> Some economists suggest this bunching effect can amplify market volatility and reduce the stabilizing influence of continuous trading.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Blouin |first1=Jennifer L. |last2=Raedy |first2=Jana Smith |last3=Shackelford |first3=Douglas A. |date=2003-09-01 |title=Capital Gains Taxes and Equity Trading: Empirical Evidence |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1475-679X.00118 |journal=Journal of Accounting Research |language=en |volume=41 |issue=4 |pages=611–651 |doi=10.1111/1475-679X.00118 |issn=0021-8456|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Revenue and distribution ==

=== Contribution to total tax revenue ===
In the United States, capital gains tax receipts have historically represented a modest and variable share of federal revenue. According to the [[Congressional Budget Office]], such receipts are typically between 2% and 3% of total federal receipts, and normally account for approximately 4% to 7% of individual income tax revenues, though the proportion fluctuates significantly with asset market conditions.<ref>{{cite report |url=https://www.cbo.gov/sites/default/files/107th-congress-2001-2002/reports/taxbrief2.pdf |title=Capital Gains Taxes and Federal Revenues |author=Congressional Budget Office |date=October 9, 2002 |access-date=2026-05-19 |series=Revenue and Tax Policy Brief}}</ref> Revenue from this source remains modest relative to income and payroll taxes, reflecting the concentrated ownership of capital assets among higher-income taxpayers.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Burman |first1=Leonard E. |last2=Geissler |first2=Christopher |last3=Toder |first3=Eric J. |date=2008 |title=How Big Are Total Individual Income Tax Expenditures, and Who Benefits from Them? |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/29729999 |journal=The American Economic Review |volume=98 |issue=2 |pages=79–83 |doi=10.1257/aer.98.2.79 |jstor=29729999 |issn=0002-8282}}</ref>

=== Burden across income levels ===
Capital gains tax liability is highly concentrated among high-income taxpayers; in the United States, the top 1% of earners have accounted for approximately 75% of total capital gains tax paid.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Burman |first1=Leonard E. |last2=Clausing |first2=Kimberly A. |last3=Austin |first3=Lydia |date=September 2017 |title=Is U.S. Corporate Income Double-Taxed? |url=https://taxpolicycenter.org/sites/default/files/publication/144606/2001514-is-u.s.-corporate-income-double-taxed_0.pdf |journal=National Tax Journal |volume=70 |issue=3 |pages=675–706 |doi=10.17310/ntj.2017.3.06 |access-date=2026-05-19}}</ref> This concentration reflects the unequal distribution of capital assets rather than rate progressivity alone, as middle-income households hold most of their wealth in primary residences, which are often exempt or treated separately.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Baranes |first1=Avraham I. |last2=Brown |first2=Lawrence |date=2023 |title=Labor Relations in a Post-COVID Economy: The Great Resignation through the Lens of Institutional Adjustment |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/00213624.2023.2202141 |journal=Journal of Economic Issues |volume=57 |issue=2 |pages=567–574 |doi=10.1080/00213624.2023.2202141 |access-date=2026-05-19|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The effective burden also varies based on asset composition, with higher-income investors generally having greater access to tax planning strategies.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Piketty |first1=Thomas |last2=Saez |first2=Emmanuel |date=February 2003 |title=Income Inequality in the United States, 1913–1998 |url=https://eml.berkeley.edu/~saez/pikettyqje.pdf |journal=The Quarterly Journal of Economics |volume=118 |issue=1 |pages=1–39 |doi=10.1162/00335530360535135 |access-date=2026-05-19}}</ref>

=== Wealth concentration ===
The relationship between capital gains taxation and wealth concentration is debated. Higher rates may limit wealth accumulation through asset appreciation, while the preferential treatment of investment income relative to wage income has been argued to advantage those who derive income primarily from capital.<ref>{{cite report |url=https://eml.berkeley.edu/~saez/saez-zucmanNBER14wealth.pdf |title=Wealth Inequality in the United States since 1913: Evidence from Capitalized Income Tax Data |last1=Saez |first1=Emmanuel |last2=Zucman |first2=Gabriel |date=October 2014 |publisher=National Bureau of Economic Research |access-date=2026-05-19 |number=Working Paper 20625}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Piketty |first=Thomas |url=https://dowbor.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/06/14Thomas-Piketty.pdf |title=Capital in the Twenty-First Century |date=2014 |publisher=The Belknap Press of Harvard University Press |isbn=978-0-674-43000-6 |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts |translator=Goldhammer, Arthur |access-date=2026-05-19}}</ref> Exemptions for primary residences and retirement accounts provide wealth-building opportunities across income levels, while sophisticated tax planning strategies tend to be more accessible to high-net-worth investors.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kopczuk |first=Wojciech |date=2015-02-01 |title=What Do We Know about the Evolution of Top Wealth Shares in the United States? |journal=Journal of Economic Perspectives |language=en |volume=29 |issue=1 |pages=47–66 |doi=10.1257/jep.29.1.47 |doi-access=free |issn=0895-3309}}</ref>

=== Intergenerational equity ===
Capital gains taxation intersects with intergenerational wealth transfer through the treatment of inherited assets. In the United States, step-up basis provisions reset the cost basis of inherited assets to their value at the time of the owner's death, eliminating any capital gains tax on appreciation during the decedent's lifetime.<ref>{{cite report |url=https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w7811/w7811.pdf |title=The Distributional Burden of Taxing Estates and Unrealized Capital Gains at the Time of Death |last1=Poterba |first1=James M. |last2=Weisbenner |first2=Scott J. |date=July 2000 |publisher=National Bureau of Economic Research |access-date=2026-05-19 |number=Working Paper 7811}}</ref> This has been characterized by some as advantaging wealthy families able to hold assets until death, compared with those who must realize gains during their lifetime. The overall burden on intergenerational wealth transfer depends on the interaction between capital gains and estate tax systems.<ref>{{cite report |url=https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w8205/w8205.pdf |title=Rethinking the Estate and Gift Tax: Overview |last1=Gale |first1=William G. |last2=Slemrod |first2=Joel B. |date=2001 |publisher=National Bureau of Economic Research |access-date=2026-05-19 |number=Working Paper 8205}}</ref>

== Impact on entrepreneurship ==
Capital gains taxation affects the after-tax returns to successful business ventures and startup investments, which some argue discourages risk-taking.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Da Rin |first1=Marco |last2=Nicodano |first2=Giovanna |last3=Sembenelli |first3=Alessandro |date=September 2006 |title=Public Policy and the Creation of Active Venture Capital Markets |url=https://pure.uvt.nl/ws/files/771176/DaRin-Nicodano-Sembenelli.pdf |journal=Journal of Public Economics |volume=90 |issue=8–9 |pages=1699–1723 |doi=10.1016/j.jpubeco.2005.09.013 |hdl=2318/99556 |access-date=2026-05-19}}</ref> Policy recognition of this concern is reflected in provisions such as the qualified small business stock exclusion in the United States, which offers preferential treatment to offset investment risks.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Accelerating Energy Innovation: Insights from Multiple Sectors 9780226326856 |url=https://dokumen.pub/accelerating-energy-innovation-insights-from-multiple-sectors-9780226326856.html |access-date=2026-05-19 |website=dokumen.pub |language=en}}</ref> The timing of capital gains recognition may also influence decisions about when entrepreneurs sell businesses or take companies public.<ref>{{Cite SSRN |last1=MacIntosh |first1=Jeffrey G. |last2=Cumming |first2=Douglas J. |date=February 2002 |title=Venture Capital Exits in Canada and the United States |ssrn=321641 |ssrn-access=free}}</ref>

== Compliance and administration ==

=== Tax return filing obligations ===
In most jurisdictions, taxpayers are required to report capital gains and losses on designated tax forms within specified timeframes following the tax year in which the disposal occurred. Annual reporting is generally required regardless of whether gains or losses were realized, with specific schedules dedicated to capital transactions.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Prior year forms and instructions {{!}} Internal Revenue Service |url=https://www.irs.gov/prior-year-forms-and-instructions,%20https://www.irs.gov/prior-year-forms-and-instructions |access-date=2026-05-19 |website=www.irs.gov |language=en}}</ref> Reporting obligations typically extend to all qualifying asset disposals including securities, real estate, and business assets, with different forms used for different asset categories depending on the jurisdiction's tax structure.

=== Record-keeping requirements ===
Taxpayers are generally required to report capital gains and losses on designated forms within specified timeframes following the tax year of disposal, with most jurisdictions requiring annual reporting through dedicated schedules.<ref name=":3" /> Comprehensive records must be maintained for all capital asset transactions – including acquisition dates, costs, improvement expenses, and disposal details — for minimum periods typically ranging from three to seven years after the relevant filing date.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Capital gains tax reporting |url=https://www.litrg.org.uk/savings-property/capital-gains-tax/capital-gains-tax-reporting |access-date=2026-05-19 |website=www.litrg.org.uk}}</ref>

=== Disclosure of foreign assets ===
International tax compliance in many jurisdictions requires disclosure of foreign capital assets and related gains through specialized reporting forms capturing cross-border transactions. Taxpayers holding foreign securities, real estate, or business interests above specified thresholds may be required to file additional schedules detailing asset locations, values, and disposal proceeds.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR) |url=https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/report-of-foreign-bank-and-financial-accounts-fbar |access-date=2026-05-19 |website=www.irs.gov |language=en}}</ref>

=== Administrative expenses ===
With collecting of any type of [[tax]] come administrative costs associated with collecting, administering and managing the collection of capital gains taxes. These costs are directly incurred by governments that collect taxes, and ultimately its citizens. Unfortunately, no studies (at least that [[Fraser Institute]] researchers knew of in 2007) specifically analyze the costs associated with capital gains taxes.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Veldhuis|first1=Niels|last2=Godin|first2=Keith|last3=Clemens|first3=Jason|date=February 2007|title=The Economic Costs of Capital Gains Taxes|url=https://www.fraserinstitute.org/sites/default/files/EconomicCostsCapitalGainsTax.pdf|journal=Studies in Entrepreneurship Markets|volume=4|pages=18–20|via=Fraser Institute}}</ref>

Canadian researcher Francois Vailancourt<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=ZQHFbzsAAAAJ&hl=en | title=François Vaillancourt }}</ref> in 1989 examines the administrative costs associated with personal income taxes and two payroll taxes (CPP/QPP and UI). The costs include processing costs, administration and accommodation costs, capital expenses, and litigation costs. These costs represented '''''roughly 1% of the gross revenues collected''''' by these three tax sources. The paper does not show exactly what costs are incurred by capital gains tax.

=== Compliance costs ===
Tax compliance costs are incurred when fulfilling the recording and filing requirements associated with paying a tax. These costs include such expenses as bookkeeping, reporting, calculating, and remitting tax payments. A study from 1992, which may be outdated due to technological advancements, found that American taxpayers who received capital gains income incurred higher compliance costs than those who did not.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Blumenthal |first1=Marsha |last2=Slemrod |first2=Joel |title=The Compliance Cost of the U.S. Individual Income Tax System: A Second Look After Tax Reform |date=June 1992 |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1086/NTJ41788959?journalCode=ntj |journal=National Tax Journal |volume=45 |issue=2|pages=185–202 |doi=10.1086/NTJ41788959 |s2cid=232211587 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> From a survey of 2,000 [[Minnesota]] households, the authors found that having capital gains increased the time individuals spent on paying taxes by 7.9 hours, increased the money they spent on professional tax assistance by about $21, and increased the total cost of compliance by $143 per taxpayer (not adjusted for inflation) per year.<ref name=":0" />

Altogether the study concludes that very few studies measure compliance costs associated with capital gains tax, but those few that do clearly indicate that compliance costs are not insignificant. Therefore, the costs must be taken into consideration when assessing tax policy.

=== Tax avoidance or deferrence ===
Taxpayers may defer capital gains taxes by simply deferring the sale of the asset. Depending on the specifics of national tax law, taxpayers may be able to legally reduce, or [[tax avoidance|avoid capital gains taxes]] using the following strategies:

*A nation may tax at a lower rate the gains on investments in favored industries or sectors, such as small business.
*Tax can be reduced when property ownership is transferred to family members in the low-income bracket. In the U.S., if in the year of selling the property a taxpayer's family member falls within the 10% to 12% ordinary income tax bracket, they could avoid the capital gains tax entirely.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.investopedia.com/articles/personal-finance/101515/comparing-longterm-vs-shortterm-capital-gain-tax-rates.asp/|title=Understanding Long-Term vs. Short-Term Capital Gains|last1=Boyte-White |first1=Claire |website=investopedia.com}}</ref>
*There may be accounts with tax-favored status. The most advantageous of these let gains accumulate in the account without taxes; however, taxes may be owed when the taxpayer withdraws funds from the account.
*Selling an asset at a loss may create a "tax loss" that can be applied to offset gains realized in the future, and avoid or reduce taxes on those gains. Tax losses are a business asset, but the business must avoid [[Tax shelter#Judicial doctrines to combat tax shelters|"sham" transactions]], such as selling to oneself or a subsidiary for no legitimate purpose other than to create a tax loss.
*Tax may be waived if the asset is given to a charity.
*Tax may be deferred if the taxpayer sells the asset but receives payment from the buyer over a period of years. However, the taxpayer bears the risk of a default by the buyer during that period. A [[structured sale]] or purchase of an [[Life annuity|annuity]] may be ways to defer taxes.
*In certain transactions, the basis (original cost) of the asset is changed. In the U.S., the basis for an inherited asset becomes its value at the time of the inheritance.
*Tax may be deferred if the seller of an asset puts the funds into the purchase of a "like-kind" asset. In the U.S., this is called a [[Internal Revenue Code section 1031|1031 exchange]] and is now generally available only for business-related real estate and tangible property.
*Tax may be deferred if the capital gain income is reinvested into certain geographic areas. In the U.S., the [[Opportunity Zone]] program was created to "recycle capital into the economy that would otherwise be 'frozen' in place due to investors' reluctance to trigger capital gains taxes" and "bring investment and development to lower income areas that do not otherwise receive a great deal of attention".<ref>{{cite web |last1=Brezski |first1=Jan |title=Opportunity Zone Investment vs 1031 Exchanges |url=https://www.arixacapital.com/opportunity-zone-investment-vs-1031-exchange |website=arixacapital.com/ |access-date=15 January 2019 |archive-date=12 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112002429/https://www.arixacapital.com/opportunity-zone-investment-vs-1031-exchange/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

=== Tax evasion ===
Capital gains taxes have also led some taxpayers to illegally evade the payment of the tax. The level of [[tax evasion]] is the extent to which actual tax revenue collected by government differs from that which would have been collected if every taxpayer paid exactly what is required by law. Tax evasion has important implications for the [[Tax efficiency|efficiency]] of taxes, since resources spent on evading the tax could be put to more productive uses.<ref name=":0" />

Professor [[James M. Poterba|James Poterba's]] work from 1987 in the [[American Economic Review]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Poterba |first1=James M. |title=Tax Evasion and Capital Gains Taxation |journal=The American Economic Review |date=1987 |volume=77 |issue=2 |pages=234–239 |jstor=1805456 }}</ref> studied the relationship between capital gains taxes and tax evasion: a 1% decrease in capital gains tax rate increases the reported tax base by 0.4% (amounting to a 0.6% decrease in tax collected).

A more recent study from the ''[[Journal of Public Economics]]''<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Landsman |first1=Wayne R |last2=Shackelford |first2=Douglas A |last3=Yetman |first3=Robert J |title=The determinants of capital gains tax compliance: evidence from the RJR Nabisco leveraged buyout |journal=Journal of Public Economics |date=April 2002 |volume=84 |issue=1 |pages=47–74 |doi=10.1016/S0047-2727(01)00099-8 }}</ref> provides support for Poterba's work with evidence from a unique data set of shareholder information from the 1989 leveraged buyout of [[RJR Nabisco]]. The study estimates that a one percentage-point increase in the marginal tax rate on capital gains is associated with a 0.42% increase in evasion (amounting to a 0.58% increase in tax collected). In addition, the authors find that the average level of evasion was 11% of the total capital gains.

==By country==

=== Albania ===
In [[Albania]], capital gains on the sale of stocks or shares are taxable at 15%. This tax rate also applies to capital gains made from transfers of ownership of real estate, both land or buildings. Individual income tax rate on dividends is 8%.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Albania - Individual - Income determination |url=https://taxsummaries.pwc.com/albania/individual/income-determination |access-date=2022-04-22 |website=taxsummaries.pwc.com |language=en-gb}}</ref>

===Argentina===
There is no specific capital gains tax in [[Argentina]]; however, there is a 9% to 35% tax for fiscal residents on their world revenues, including capital gains.{{Citation needed|date=March 2009}}

===Australia===
{{main|Capital gains tax in Australia}}

[[Australia]] collects capital gains tax only upon realized capital gains, except for certain provisions relating to deferred-interest [[debt]] such as [[zero-coupon bond]]s. The tax is not separate in its own right, but forms part of the [[income tax|income-tax]] system. The proceeds of an asset sold less its "cost base" (the original cost plus additions for cost price increases over time) are the capital gain. Discounts and other concessions apply to certain taxpayers in varying circumstances. Capital gains tax is collected from assets anywhere in the world, not only in Australia.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ato.gov.au/General/Capital-gains-tax/?default|title=Capital gains tax|last=Office|first=Australian Taxation|website=ato.gov.au|language=en-AU|access-date=12 April 2019}}</ref>

Capital gains tax (CGT) is the levy applied to profits from selling assets. Despite its designation as "capital gains tax", it is not a standalone tax but rather a constituent part of Australia's income tax. When assets are sold (typically upon ceasing ownership), a CGT event is triggered, and capital gains and losses must be disclosed in the income tax return.

From 21 September 1999, after a report by [[Alan Reynolds (economist)|Alan Reynolds]], the 50% capital gains tax discount has been in place for individuals and for some trusts that acquired the asset after that time and that have held the asset for more than 12 months, however the tax is levied without any adjustment to the cost base for inflation. The amount left after applying the discount is added to the assessable income of the taxpayer for that financial year.

For individuals, the most significant exemption is the principal [[family home]] when not used for business purposes such as rental income or home-based business activity. The sale of personal residential property is normally exempt from capital gains tax, except for gains realized during any period in which the property was unused as a personal residence (for example, while leased to other tenants) or portions attributable to business use. Capital gains or losses as a general rule can be disregarded for CGT purposes when assets were acquired before 20 September 1985 (pre-CGT).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ato.gov.au/General/property/your-home/|title=Property|last=Office|first=Australian Taxation|website=ato.gov.au|language=en-AU|access-date=26 August 2019}}</ref>

===Austria===
[[Austria]] taxes capital gains at 25% (on checking account and "Sparbuch" interest) or 27.5% (all other types of capital gains). There is an exception for capital gains from the sale of shares of foreign entities (with opaque taxation) if the participation exceeds 10% and shares are held for over one year (so-called "Schachtelprivileg").<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bmf.gv.at/steuern/Besteuerung-inl-sowie-im-Inland-bez-Kapitalertraege.html |title=Besteuerung inländischer sowie im Inland bezogener Kapitalerträge |publisher=BMF |date=14 June 2018 |access-date=26 September 2018}}</ref>

=== Belarus ===
In [[Belarus]], capital gains are included in the total income of the individual taxpayer. Income from the sale of one house, apartment, building, land plot, garage and a car parking space within 5 years and more is not taxable. However, income from the second sale and every subsequent sale of an immovable property of the same type within a five-year period is fully taxable.

Income derived from the disposal of one vehicle within a calendar year is exempted from PIT, but is subject to PIT with standard terms for every subsequent disposal of a vehicle.

Income derived from the disposal of shares in a statutory capital of a Belarusian company is exempted from PIT as long as the taxpayer was in possession of these shares for a continuous period of no less than three years.

Income derived from the sale of securities is subject to PIT in compliance with the Tax Code.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Belarus - Individual - Income determination |url=https://taxsummaries.pwc.com/belarus/individual/income-determination |access-date=2022-04-22 |website=taxsummaries.pwc.com |language=en-gb |archive-date=23 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210923064133/https://taxsummaries.pwc.com/belarus/individual/income-determination |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The capital gains tax rate in Belarus is 18% for disposal of stocks/shares.

===Belgium===
Under the participation exemption, capital gains realised by a Belgian resident company on shares in a Belgian or foreign company are fully exempt from corporate income tax, provided that the dividends on the shares qualify for the participation exemption. For purposes of the participation exemption for capital gains the minimum participation test is not required.
Unrealised capital gains on shares that are recognised in the financial statements (which recognition is not mandatory) are taxable. But a roll-over relief is granted if, and as long as, the gain is booked in a separate reserve account on the balance sheet and is not used for distribution or allocation of any kind.

As a counterpart to the new exemption of realised capital gains, capital losses on shares, both realised and unrealised, are no longer tax deductible. However, the loss incurred in connection with the liquidation of a subsidiary company remains deductible up to the amount of the paid-up share capital.

Other capital gains are taxed at the ordinary rate. If the total amount of sales is used for the purchase of depreciable fixed assets within 3 years, the taxation of the capital gains will be spread over the depreciable period of these assets.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://economie.fgov.be/investors/why_invest_in_belgium/tax.htm#5 |title=Invest in Belgium |work=economie.fgov.be |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080328005907/http://economie.fgov.be/investors/why_invest_in_belgium/tax.htm |archive-date=28 March 2008 }}</ref>

===Brazil===
Capital gain taxes are only paid on realized gains. At the current stage, taxes are 15% for transactions longer than one-day-old and 20% for day trading, both transactions are due payable at the following month after selling or closing the position. Dividends are tax free, since the issuer company has already paid to ''[[Receita Federal do Brasil|RECEITA FEDERAL]]'' (the Brazilian tax office). Derivatives (futures and options) follow the same rules for tax purposes as company stocks. When selling less than R$20.000 ([[Brazilian Real|Brazilian Reais]]) within a month (and not operating in day trading), the financial operation is considered tax-free. Also, non-residents have no tax on capital gains.<ref name=Brazilian>{{cite web|url=http://www.cvm.gov.br/ingl/indexing.asp|website=CVM – Comissão de Valores Mobiliários (Brazilian SEC)|title=Securities and Exchange Commission of Brazil|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100410175904/http://www.cvm.gov.br/ingl/indexing.asp|archive-date=10 April 2010}}</ref>

===Bulgaria===
The Corporate tax rate is 10%.
The personal tax rate is flat at 10%.
There is no capital gains tax on equity instruments traded on the BSE.

===Canada===
A Capital Gains tax was first introduced in Canada by [[Pierre Trudeau]] and his finance minister [[Edgar Benson]] in the [[1971 Canadian federal budget]].<ref name=":LeaderPost">{{Cite web|date= 19 June 1971 |title=The Leader-Post|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=w9EjUEod0xMC&dat=19710619&printsec=frontpage&hl=fr|access-date=17 June 2020}}</ref>

Some exceptions apply, such as selling one's primary residence which may be exempt from taxation.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cra-arc.gc.ca/tx/ndvdls/tpcs/ncm-tx/rtrn/cmpltng/rprtng-ncm/lns101-170/127/rsdnc/dspsng/menu-eng.html|title=CRA|work=cra-arc.gc.ca|date=27 November 2019}}</ref> Capital gains made by investments in a [[Tax-Free Savings Account]] (TFSA) are not taxed.

Since the [[2013 Canadian federal budget|2013 budget]], interest can no longer be claimed as a capital gain. The formula is the same for capital losses and these can be carried forward indefinitely to offset future years' capital gains; capital losses not used in the current year can also be carried back to the previous three tax years to offset capital gains tax paid in those years.

Profitable sales of assets result in either capital gains (included in income at a rate of 50%) or income from a business (included fully in income). Characterization depends on a number of criteria, and varies based on the type of assets disposed of. Sales of securities typically result in capital gains, although "trading" securities with e.g. short holding periods, frequent transactions, or where they constitute a large share of one's income suggests business income.<ref>{{cite web |title=IT-479R Transactions in securities |date=6 September 2002 |url=https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/forms-publications/publications/it479r/archived-transactions-securities.html |publisher=CRA}}</ref> In the case of other assets, sales are "income account" when they are purchased to be sold, particularly in a short time, whereas sales of assets acquired for personal use or to generate income are on "capital account".<ref>{{cite web |title=IT-218R Profit, Capital Gains and Losses from the Sale of Real Estate, Including Farmland and Inherited Land and Conversion of Real Estate from Capital Property to Inventory and Vice Versa |date=8 January 2013 |url=https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/technical-information/income-tax/income-tax-folios-index/series-1-individuals/folio-3-family-unit-issues/income-tax-folio-s1-f3-c2-principal-residence.html |publisher=CRA}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |title=IT-459 Adventure or Concern in the Nature of Trade |date=8 September 1980 |url=https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/forms-publications/publications/it459/archived-adventure-concern-nature-trade.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250307172101/https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/forms-publications/publications/it459/archived-adventure-concern-nature-trade.html |archive-date=7 March 2025 |publisher=[[Canada Revenue Agency]]}}</ref>

For corporations as for individuals, 50% of realized capital gains are taxable. The net taxable capital gains (which can be calculated as 50% of total capital gains minus 50% of total capital losses) are subject to income tax at normal corporate tax rates. If more than 50% of a small business's income is derived from specified investment business activities (which include income from capital gains) they are not permitted to claim the small business deduction.

Capital gains earned on income in a [[Registered Retirement Savings Plan]] are not taxed at the time the gain is realized (i.e., when the holder sells a stock that has appreciated inside of their RRSP) but they are taxed when the funds are withdrawn from the registered plan (usually after being converted to a Registered Income Fund at the age of 71). These gains are then taxed at the individual's full marginal rate.

Capital gains earned on income in a TFSA are not taxed at the time the gain is realized. Any money withdrawn from a TFSA, including capital gains, are also not taxed.

Unrealized capital gains are generally not taxed, except for the deemed disposition when emigrating out of Canada or inheritance by a non-spouse.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Agency|first=Canada Revenue|date=1999-11-01|title=Leaving Canada (emigrants)|url=https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/international-non-residents/individuals-leaving-entering-canada-non-residents/leaving-canada-emigrants.html#dptx|access-date=2021-02-25|website=aem}}</ref>

In 2022, with price levels surging, some economists have argued that the capital gain tax should be adjusted for inflation, saying that without such adjustment, it taxes "fictional gains", which discourages investment.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Brethour |first=Patrick |date=2022-04-18 |title=How to keep inflation and taxes from devouring capital gains |language=en-CA |work=The Globe and Mail |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/investing/personal-finance/taxes/article-how-to-keep-inflation-and-taxes-from-devouring-capital-gains/ |access-date=2022-04-22}}</ref>

===China===
{{Unreferenced section|date=May 2014}}
The applicable tax rate for capital gains in [[China]] depends upon the nature of the taxpayer (i.e. whether the taxpayer is a person or company) and whether the taxpayer is resident or non-resident for tax purposes. It should however be noted that, unlike common law tax systems, Chinese income tax legislation does not provide a distinction between income and capital. What is commonly referred to by taxpayers and practitioners as capital gain tax is actually within the income tax framework, rather than a separate regime.

Tax-resident enterprises will be taxed at 25% in accordance with the Enterprise Income Tax Law. Non-resident enterprises will be taxed at 10% on capital gains in accordance with the Implementing Regulations to the Enterprise Income Tax Law. In practice, where a resident of a treaty partner alienates assets situated in China as part of its ordinary course of business the gains so derived will likely be assessed as if it is a capital gain, rather than business profit. This is somewhat contradictory with the basic principles of double taxation treaty.

The only tax circular specifically addressing the PRC income tax treatment of income derived by QFIIs from the holding and trading of Chinese securities is Guo Shui Han (2009) No.47 ("Circular 47") issued by the State Administration of Taxation ("SAT") on 23 January 2009. The circular addresses the withholding tax treatment of dividends and interest received by QFIIs from PRC resident companies, however, circular 47 is silent on the treatment of capital gains derived by QFIIs on the trading of A-shares. It is generally accepted that Circular 47 is intentionally silent on capital gains and a possible indication that SAT is considering, but still undecided on, whether to grant tax exemption or other concessionary treatment to capital gains derived by QFIIs. Nevertheless, it is noted that there have been cases where QFIIs withdraw capital from China after paying 10% withholding tax on gains derived through share trading over the years on a transaction-by-transaction basis. This uncertainty has caused significant problems for those investment managers investing in A-Shares. Guo Shui Han (2009) No. 698 ("Circular 698") was issued on 10 December 2009 addressing the PRC corporate income tax treatment on the transfer of PRC equity interest by non-PRC tax resident enterprises directly or indirectly, however has not resolved the uncertain tax position with regards A-Shares. With respect to Circular 698 itself, there are views that it is not consistent with the Enterprise Income Tax Law as well as double taxation treaties signed by the Chinese government. The validity of the Circular is controversial, especially in light of recent developments in the international arena, such as the TPG case in Australia and [[Vodafone]] case in India.

=== Colombia ===
Under Colombian law, there are different kinds of capital gains subject to taxation:
* Gains derived from the sale of assets (shares, bonds, etc.) held for a minimum of 2 years.
* Gains derived from the liquidation of a company that has been in existence for a minimum of 2 years.
* Gains derived from inheritances, donations or legacies (portion of estate received by spouse or heir)
* Gains derived from gambling and lotteries
The general capital gains tax rate in [[Colombia]] is 10%, with the exception of lottery or gambling winnings, which are taxed at 20%.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Colombia - Individual - Other taxes |url=https://taxsummaries.pwc.com/colombia/individual/other-taxes |access-date=2022-04-22 |website=taxsummaries.pwc.com |language=en-gb}}</ref>

===Croatia===
The capital gains tax in [[Croatia]] is 10%. It was introduced in 2015 at a rate of 12% and reduced to 10% in 2021.
===Cyprus===
In Cyprus, capital gains tax (CGT) applies to gains connected with immovable property situated in Cyprus where the disposal is not subject to income tax. For CGT purposes, a disposal may include a sale, exchange, lease, gift, abandonment of a right, grant of a right to purchase, or compensation received following the cancellation of a disposal.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cyprus - Individual - Other taxes |url=https://taxsummaries.pwc.com/cyprus/individual/other-taxes |website=PwC}}</ref>

CGT is imposed at a rate of 20% on gains arising from the disposal of immovable property situated in Cyprus. It may also apply to the disposal of shares in companies that directly own Cyprus immovable property and to shares in companies that indirectly own such property. In the case of a share disposal, the taxable gain is restricted to the part attributable to the Cyprus immovable property.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cyprus - Individual - Other taxes |url=https://taxsummaries.pwc.com/cyprus/individual/other-taxes |website=PwC}}</ref>

From 1 January 2026, an indirect disposal of shares may be subject to CGT where at least 20% of the market value of the shares is derived from immovable property situated in Cyprus. The previous threshold was 50%. The exemption concerning shares listed on a recognised stock exchange was replaced by an exemption for shares listed on a regulated stock exchange. Transitional protection applies to certain shares acquired before 1 January 2026. No CGT is imposed on shares listed on a non-regulated stock exchange where the total disposal amount does not exceed €50,000 during the relevant tax year.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cyprus enacts major tax reform legislation |url=https://globaltaxnews.ey.com/news/2026-0140-cyprus-enacts-major-tax-reform-legislation |website=Ernst & Young}}</ref>

The taxable gain is generally calculated by deducting the acquisition cost, qualifying improvement expenditure and certain expenses connected with the acquisition and disposal from the disposal proceeds. The acquisition cost and qualifying improvements may be adjusted for inflation using the Cyprus consumer price index. For property acquired before 1 January 1980, the acquisition cost is generally based on the property's value on that date.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cyprus - Individual - Other taxes |url=https://taxsummaries.pwc.com/cyprus/individual/other-taxes |website=PwC}}</ref>

Individuals may claim lifetime exemptions against taxable capital gains. From 1 January 2026, these include up to €150,000 for the disposal of a qualifying principal residence, €50,000 for agricultural land disposed of by a farmer and €30,000 for other qualifying disposals. The exemptions are subject to an overall lifetime maximum of €150,000.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cyprus - Individual - Other taxes |url=https://taxsummaries.pwc.com/cyprus/individual/other-taxes |website=PwC}}</ref>

Further exemptions may apply, subject to statutory conditions, to certain gifts between close relatives, transfers on death, donations to approved charities, qualifying corporate reorganisations and specified exchanges of property. Land and buildings acquired at market value from unrelated parties between 16 July 2015 and 31 December 2016 may also qualify for an exemption on a subsequent disposal.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cyprus - Individual - Other taxes |url=https://taxsummaries.pwc.com/cyprus/individual/other-taxes |website=PwC}}</ref>

===Czech Republic===
Capital gains in the [[Czech Republic]] are taxed as income for companies and individuals. The Czech income tax rate for an individual's income in 2010 is a flat 15% rate. Corporate tax in 2024 is 21%. Capital gains from the sale of shares by a company owning 10% or more is entitled to participation exemption under certain terms. For an individual, gain from the sale of a primary private dwelling, held for at least 3<ref>{{Cite web|title=Daňový portál: Časový test – Daň z příjmů fyzických osob|url=https://www.mesec.cz/danovy-portal/dan-z-prijmu/casovy-test/|access-date=2021-04-26|website=Měšec.cz|language=cs}}</ref> years, is tax exempt. Or, when not used as a main residence, if held for more than 10 years. Any capital gains realized on the disposal of securities up to annual gross sale amount of [[Czech koruna|CZK]] 100,000 are tax exempt for the taxpayer.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-03-16|title=Czech Republic – Income Tax – KPMG Global|url=https://home.kpmg/xx/en/home/insights/2014/01/czech-republic-income-tax.html|access-date=2021-04-26|website=KPMG|language=en-US|archive-date=26 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210426155417/https://home.kpmg/xx/en/home/insights/2014/01/czech-republic-income-tax.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Denmark===
Share dividends and realized capital gains on shares are charged 27% to individuals of gains up to DKK 48,300 (2013-level, adjusted annually), and at 42% of gains above that.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.skat.dk/SKAT.aspx?oId=1549830 |title=SKAT: Satser og belřbsgrćnser 2010+2011 |publisher=Skat.dk |access-date=9 February 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120318011449/http://www.skat.dk/SKAT.aspx?oId=1549830 |archive-date=18 March 2012  }}</ref> Carryforward of realized losses on shares is allowed.

Individuals' interest income from bank deposits and bonds, realized gains on property and other capital gains are taxed up to 59%, however, several exemptions occur, such as on selling one's principal private residence or on gains on selling bonds. Interest paid on loans is deductible, although in case the net capital income is negative, only approx. 33% tax credit applies.

Companies are taxed at 25%. Share dividends are taxed at 28%.

===Ecuador===
{{Unreferenced section|date=May 2014}}

'''Corporate taxation:'''

Residence for tax purposes is based on the place of incorporation.

Resident entities are taxed on worldwide income. Nonresidents are subject to tax only on Ecuador-source income.

Capital gains are treated as ordinary income and taxed at the normal corporate rate.

The standard rate is 22%, with a reduced rate of 15% applying where corporate profits are reinvested for the purchase of machinery or equipment and/or the acquisition of new technology. Companies engaged in the exploration or exploitation of hydrocarbon also are subject to the standard corporate tax rate.

'''Personal taxation:'''

Resident individuals are taxed on their worldwide income; nonresidents are taxed only on Ecuadorian-source income.

An individual is deemed to be resident if they are in [[Ecuador]] for more than 6 months in a year.

Capital gains are treated as ordinary income and taxed at the normal rate.

Rates are progressive from 0% to 35%.

===Egypt===
After the [[Egyptian Revolution of 2011|Egyptian Revolution]], there was a proposal for a 10% capital gains tax.
This proposal was implemented on 29 May 2014.
Egypt exempt bonus shares from a new 10 percent capital gains tax on profits made on the stock market as the country's Finance Minister Hany Dimian said on 30 May 2014, and distributions of bonus shares will be exempt from the taxes, and the new tax will not be retroactive.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20140602200244/http://af.reuters.com/article/egyptNews/idAFL6N0OG28120140530 Reuters]</ref>

===Estonia===
{{Unreferenced section|date=March 2026}}
There is no separate capital gains tax in [[Estonia]]. For residents of Estonia all capital gains are taxed the same as regular income, the rate of which currently stands at 20%. Resident natural persons that have investment account can realize capital gains on some classes of assets tax free until withdrawal of funds from the investment account. For resident legal persons (includes partnerships) no tax is payable for realizing capital gain (or receiving any other type of income), but only on payment of dividends, payments from capital (exceeding contributions to capital) and payments not related to business. The income tax rate for resident legal persons is 20% (payment of 80 units of dividends triggers 20 units of tax due).

===Finland===
The capital gains tax in [[Finland]] is 30% on realized capital income and 34% if the realized capital income is over 30,000 euros.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://portal.vero.fi/public/default.aspx?nodeid=9768&culture=en-US&contentlan=2 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160106194154/http://portal.vero.fi/public/default.aspx?nodeid=9768&culture=en-US&contentlan=2 |url-status=dead |archive-date=6 January 2016 |title=Tax Guide, Individuals 2015 |publisher=vero.fi |date=10 March 2014 |access-date=22 April 2015 }}</ref> The capital gains tax in 2011 was 28% on realized capital income.<ref>VERO [http://www.vero.fi/default.asp?article=3619&domain=VERO_ENGLISH&path=488,489&language=ENG Taxation of Stock Options] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110514034032/http://www.vero.fi/default.asp?article=3619&domain=VERO_ENGLISH&path=488%2C489&language=ENG |date=14 May 2011 }}</ref> Carryforward of realized losses is allowed for five years. However, capital gains from the sale of residential homes is tax-free after two years of residence, with certain limitations.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://vero.fi/?article=2610&domain=VERO_MAIN&path=5,40&language=FIN |title=VERO |work=vero.fi |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090803085348/http://www.vero.fi/?article=2610&domain=VERO_MAIN&path=5%2C40&language=FIN |archive-date=3 August 2009  }}</ref>

Dividends from a publicly listed company are 85% taxable resulting in the CGT rate to be 25,5% or 28,9%. The company distributing the dividend will apply a 25,5% withholding tax.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.vero.fi/henkiloasiakkaat/omaisuus/sijoitukset/osakkeet_ja_osingot/ |title=Osakkeet ja osingot |work=vero.fi |access-date=18 July 2018 |archive-date=18 July 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180718204856/https://www.vero.fi/henkiloasiakkaat/omaisuus/sijoitukset/osakkeet_ja_osingot/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

===France===
{{Unreferenced section|date=May 2014}}
For residents, there are two options for treating capital gains (shares, bonds, interests, etc.). 
It was introduced by President [[Emmanuel Macron]] as a key promise of its campaign and is called the Prélèvement Forfaitaire Unique – PFU. The first option is a flat 30% rate. The second option is to opt for the former treatment whereby gains are taxed at 17.2% for "social contributions" and (if the instrument has been held for at least two years) 60% of the gains are taxed as individual revenue (tax scale between 0–45%). The following year, 6.8% of the gains can be deducted from the tax base. For equities bought after 1 January 2018, the 60% reduction for 2-year long hold does not apply anymore.

If shares are held in a special account (called a PEA), the gain is subject only to "social contributions" (17.2%) provided that the PEA is held for at least five years. The maximum amount that can be deposited in the PEA is €150,000.

The gain realized on the sale of a principal residence is not taxable. A gain realized on the sale of other real estate held at least 30 years, however, is not taxable, although this will become subject to 15.5% social security taxes as of 2012. (There is a sliding scale for non-principal residence property owned for between 22 and 30 years.)

Non-residents are generally taxable on capital gains realized on French real estate and on some French financial instruments, subject to any applicable double tax treaty. Social security taxes, however, are not usually payable by non-residents. A French tax representative will be mandatory for non-residents who sell a property for an amount over 150.000 euros or who own the real estate for more than 15 years.

===Germany===
{{Unreferenced section|date=May 2014}}
In January 2009, [[Germany]] introduced a very strict capital gains tax (called [[Flat rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)|Abgeltungsteuer]] in German) for shares, funds, certificates, bank interest rates etc. Capital gains tax only applies to financial instruments (shares, bonds etc.) that have been bought after 31 December 2008. Instruments bought before this date are exempt from capital gains tax (assuming that they have been held for at least 12 months), even if they are sold in 2009 or later, barring a change of law. Certificates are treated specially, and only qualify for tax exemption if they have been bought before 15 March 2007.

Real estate continues to be exempt from capital gains tax if it has been held for more than ten years. The German capital gains tax is 25% plus [[Taxation in Germany#Solidarity surcharge|Solidarity surcharge]] (add-on tax initially introduced to finance the five eastern states of Germany – [[Mecklenburg-Vorpommern|Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania]], [[Saxony]], [[Saxony-Anhalt]], [[Thuringia]] and [[Brandenburg]] – and the cost of the reunification, but later kept to finance all kinds of public funded projects in all Germany), plus [[Kirchensteuer]] (church tax, voluntarily), resulting in an effective tax rate of about 26.4–29%. Deductions of expenses such as custodian fees, travel to annual shareholder meetings, legal and tax advice, interest paid on loans to buy shares, etc., are no longer permitted starting in 2009.

There is an allowance ({{lang|de|Freistellungsauftrag}}) on capital gains income in Germany of €1000 per person per year tax-free, if appropriate forms are completed.

===Greece===
Transfer of non-listed shares is subject to capital gain tax at the rate of 15%. Transfer of listed shares is also taxed at 15% unless specific conditions/exemptions apply. A transfer duty of 2% is imposed on the gross sale proceeds of listed shares. Other [[Taxation in Greece|sources]] say there is no tax in the case of capital gain from trading in the stock market as long as the individual owns less than 0.5% of the publicly listed company.

Dividends distributed within taxable periods commencing after 1 January 2020 arising from entities operating under the legal form of Société Anonyme (or Limited Liability) are taxed via corporate withholding taxation at the flat rate of 5% (said rate was set to 10% for the dividends distributed during the year 2019).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://taxsummaries.pwc.com/greece/individual/income-determination|title = Greece – Individual – Income determination}}</ref>

===Hong Kong===
In general, [[Hong Kong]] has no capital gains tax. However, employees who receive shares or options as part of their [[remuneration]] are taxed at the normal Hong Kong income tax rate on the value of the shares or options at the end of any vesting period less any amount that the individual paid for the grant.

If part of the vesting period is spent outside Hong Kong, then the tax payable in Hong Kong is pro-rated based on the proportion of time spent working in Hong Kong.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gov.hk/en/residents/taxes/salaries/salariestax/chargeable/options.htm |title=How Share Awards and Share Options are Taxed |publisher=GovHK |access-date=9 February 2012}}</ref> Hong Kong has very few double tax agreements and hence there is little relief available for double taxation. Therefore, it is possible (depending on the country of origin) for employees moving to Hong Kong to pay full income tax on vested shares in both their country of origin and in Hong Kong. Similarly, an employee leaving Hong Kong can incur double taxation on the unrealized capital gains of their vested shares.

The Hong Kong taxation of capital gains on employee shares or options that are subject to a vesting period, is at odds with the treatment of unrestricted shares or options which are free of capital gains tax.

For those who do trading professionally (buying and selling securities frequently to obtain an income for living) as "traders", this will be considered income subject to personal income tax rates.

===Hungary===
Since 1 July 2023, there are two [[tax rate]]s on capital income: income tax (15%) and social security tax (13%), adding up to 28%. This includes: selling stocks, bonds, [[mutual fund]]s shares and also interests from bank [[deposit account|deposits]]. Since January 2010, Hungarian citizens can open special "long-term" accounts. The tax rate on capital gains from securities held in such an account is 10% after a three-year holding period, and 0% after the account's maximum five years period is expired. From 1 August 2013 residents also were obligated to pay an additional 6% of health insurance tax ("EHO") on their capital gain. The 6% health insurance tax on capital gains was abolished on 1 January 2017. On 1 July 2023, the government, citing the state of emergency in effect since the war in Ukraine, re-introduced an even higher 13% social security tax by decree, which was later approved by the [[Parliament]] in July 2024.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://njt.hu/jogszabaly/2023-205-20-22 |title=205/2023. (V. 31.) Gov. decree|publisher=njt.hu}}</ref>

===Iceland===

===India===
As of 2018, equities listed on recognized stock exchange are considered long term capital if the holding period is one year or more. Until 31 January 2017, all Long term capital gains from equities were exempt as per section 10 (38) if shares are sold through recognized stock exchange and [[Securities Transaction Tax]] (STT) is paid on the sale. STT in India is currently between 0.017% and 0.1% of total amount received on sale of securities through a recognized Indian stock exchange like the [[National Stock Exchange of India|NSE]] or [[Bombay Stock Exchange|BSE]]. From fiscal year 2018–2019, exemption u/s 10(38) has been withdrawn and section 112A has been introduced. The long-term capital gain shall be taxable on equities at 10% if the gain exceeds Rs. {{formatnum:100000}} as per the new section.

However, if equities are held for less than one year and is sold through recognized stock exchange then short-term capital gain is taxable at a flat rate of 15% u/s 111A and other surcharges, educational cess are imposed.(w.e.f. 1 April 2009.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://law.incometaxindia.gov.in/DitTaxmann/IncomeTaxActs/2009ITAct/ftn97section105.htm |title=ftn97section105.htm |publisher=Law.incometaxindia.gov.in |date=4 January 2009 |access-date=9 February 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120129153245/http://law.incometaxindia.gov.in/DitTaxmann/IncomeTaxActs/2009ITAct/ftn97section105.htm |archive-date=29 January 2012  }}</ref>)

In respect of immovable property, the holding period has been reduced to two years to be eligible for long term capital gain, whereas many other capital investments like jewelry are considered long term if the holding period is three or more years and are taxed at 20% u/s 112.<ref>Indian Gov [http://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/publications/4_Compute_Your_Capital_Gains/Chapter2.asp Capital Gains Tax Calculator] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140416174457/http://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/publications/4_Compute_Your_Capital_Gains/Chapter2.asp |date=16 April 2014 }}</ref>

After 2024 changes equity sales are taxed at 12.5 percent if held for more than 1 year and 20 percent if held for less than 1 year. Indexation benefit from home capital gains has been removed and the tax rate has been bought down to 12.5 percent from 20 percent.[https://www.hindustantimes.com/india-news/budget-2024-capital-gains-taxes-hiked-indexation-benefit-discontinued-101721730968342.html]
